newsitem.title: DUBAI: Iran rial slides on strong demand for hard cash.
newsitem.headline: Iran rial slides on strong demand for hard cash.

text.p: The Iranian rial has in the past few weeks weakened by more than five percent against the U.S. dollar on strong demand for hard currencies, money dealers said on Tuesday.
In Dubai, a major trading post for Iranian private business and state firms, one dollar cost 4,640 rials, up about 300 rials or seven percent on a few weeks ago, one trader said.
London-based Iranian trader Ali Pakpour said his firm was selling the dollar for up to 4,630 rials in Europe.
The German mark sold for up to 3,025 rials, sterling fetched 7,340 rials and the French franc reached an exchange rate of 890 rials, Pakpour added.
Strong demand pushed the dollar briefly to peak at 4,800 rials in Dubai and 4,750 rials in Europe late last week, the dealers said.
The Tehran newspaper Salam said on Tuesday the dollar had sold on Monday for 4,450 rials on the Tehran black market, up 200 rials in a week.
It quoted dealers as saying there was strong demand for hard currency to purchase foreign products sold at discount prices at an international trade fair held earlier this month in Tehran.
A Tehran resident said the dollar was being sold for 4,520 rials on Tuesday on the black market.

Dealers in Dubai and in Europe said some Iranian exporters were buying dollars to fulfil regulations requiring them to return their hard cash income to Iran within a few months and exchange them at the official rate of 3,000 rials to the dollar.
They said exporters, especially dealers of Persian carpets, were often unable to sell their goods within the time required for them to repatriate their hard currency income.

Iran banned free currency exchange in May 1995, setting the official exchange rate, after a drop in the value of rial to 7,000 per dollar which followed the announcement of a United States trade and investment ban against the Islamic republic.
The move led to relative stability of the rial's exchange rate after police and security agents arrested hundreds of illegal money changers, pushing the black market underground.
